description: Shared Renovate policy for every @_linked package repo in linked-fw. Edit here, not per repo: each repo's renovate.json is a three-line stub that extends this file.

statusCheckWhen.artifactError is "always" on purpose. Renovate's default is "failed": the renovate/artifacts check is created ONLY when the post-update step (running npm to regenerate package-lock.json after editing package.json) fails, and a successful run leaves no check at all. That silence is what got misread -- a PR with a package.json change and no lockfile change looked like a broken dependency, when it was npm refusing an ERESOLVE. With "always" every Renovate PR states green or red, so the absence of a lockfile change can be attributed immediately. Note the check is (re)set only on a run that commits to the branch, so PRs opened before this change keep their current state until Renovate next pushes to them.

userStrings.artifactErrorWarning: Renovate could not regenerate this repository's `package-lock.json` for this update, so the branch carries a `package.json` change with NO matching lockfile change -- that, and only that, is what a red `renovate/artifacts` check means. CI will then fail `npm ci` with `EUSAGE` ("lock file does not satisfy package.json"); that failure is NOT the new dependency breaking the code, it is the missing lockfile. Read the npm output below before anything else: if it says `ERESOLVE`, npm is correctly refusing a real peer-dependency conflict in this repo, and the fix is to resolve that conflict (or close the PR) -- never to hand-edit the lockfile.

description: THE control this whole setup exists for. Six packages' lockfiles had pinned @_linked/core 2.6.0 under a ^2.0.1 range for months; npm ci installs the lock, not the range, so xsd published shape IRIs derived from a core nobody chose. Renovate's ordinary update flow opens NOTHING there, because 2.6.0 never escaped ^2.0.1. Only lockFileMaintenance regenerates a lock that is still inside its declared range. It is disabled by default -- 'Renovate is installed' does not mean this is covered.

The fleet rule. Every @_linked/* dependency moves in ONE PR per repo, so no repo can sit on core 2.22.8 while its sibling sits on 2.6.0 -- three separate PRs merged at three different times IS the state the audit found. Automerged on green CI: an @_linked release PR exists only because someone deliberately cut that version, so a human is already upstream of it.
Peer-only @_linked deps belong in the same group and move by range replacement -- a peerDependency range that lags the dependency range is exactly how a consumer ends up resolving two cores.
React and its types move together or not at all; a split is how the JSX transform ends up mismatched between runtime and types. External, so held for review.

Third-party runtime and dev dependencies are never automerged. An @_linked bump has a deliberate human release behind it; a third party's release has nobody who reviewed it for this fleet. Held a week so a yanked version never reaches a lock.
GitHub Actions: grouped, never automerged. In .github a single bump propagates to every pipeline in the org at once, which is both the value and the risk.
Typescript alone, never grouped, never automerged. A TS minor is a compiler change and routinely breaks a build nothing else touched; when it does, the PR should say so by itself.

Majors are always solo and always human, @_linked included. Grouping majors is how one unrelated breaking change blocks nineteen safe ones -- and a core major can change emitted shape IRIs, which a green build does not catch because the build passes and only the OUTPUT is wrong.

Deferred majors: we decided not to upgrade Capacitor or Tolgee for now. Placed after the generic majors rule on purpose, so it overrides it. It stops Renovate re-raising the same major every Monday; minors and patches still flow. Each held update has a backlog note saying what breaks and what to check when it is picked up -- and in most cases the better outcome is to remove the dependency rather than upgrade it: https://github.com/linked-fw/auth/blob/main/docs/backlog/001-capacitor-dialog-8.md (replaces auth#47), https://github.com/linked-fw/auth/blob/main/docs/backlog/002-tolgee-react-7.md (replaces auth#55), https://github.com/linked-fw/server-utils/blob/main/docs/backlog/002-capacitor-core-8.md (replaces server-utils#57), https://github.com/linked-fw/shape-ui/blob/main/docs/backlog/001-capacitor-core-8.md (replaces shape-ui#36).
Lift it per package as each note is resolved; a dependency that is removed simply stops matching.

Sentry is held as a unit in linked-fw/sentry, ALL update types. @sentry/capacitor exact-pins every @sentry/* sibling and its postinstall (check-siblings) exits 1 on any other version, so no single-package Sentry PR can install there: sentry#27 (8.55.2) is unreachable under capacitor 1.x, and sentry#34 (capacitor 4) is an ERESOLVE against the pinned @sentry/react 8. All four are pinned exact, so disabling only non-patch updates would still let the #27-style patch PRs reopen. The way out is one deliberate PR moving capacitor, react, node and profiling-node together, after the Session Replay decision (Create Now backlog 051): https://github.com/linked-fw/sentry/blob/main/docs/backlog/001-sentry-capacitor-and-js-sdk-upgrade.md

Not a Capacitor coupling: every @sentry/capacitor major through 4 peers on @capacitor/core >=3.0.0, so this is independent of the Capacitor hold above. The group is kept so that deleting `enabled: false` alone yields the one combined PR this needs.
Security fixes escape both the group and the weekly schedule. Renovate ignores `schedule` here regardless; the label is the only thing this block really adds.
